metadata.title: Vijftien jaar leesprestaties in Nederland: PIRLS-2016
metadata.venue: Expertisecentrum Nederlands, Radboud Universiteit (Behavioural Science Institute)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report describes the PIRLS-2016 implementation in the Netherlands for Grade 6 reading. It states that results related to reading proficiency are based on weighted data using weighting variables provided by the international PIRLS coordination, while results from the context questionnaires are based on unweighted data. The text does not name a specific student weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT) nor does it describe replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because this is a descriptive large-scale assessment report (not an ML modeling paper), the manuscript does not provide a detailed weighting variable name or a model-based weighting procedure beyond the statement that reading proficiency estimates are weighted.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are used for PIRLS reading proficiency: the report explains that five plausible values are estimated via IRT and used as the reading proficiency score, but it does not describe how missing questionnaire/test responses were handled in the analysis. This is a reporting gap for missing-data handling because the report provides extensive sampling and scoring procedures but omits the specific missing-data rule (e.g., complete cases vs imputation) for the analytic estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample comprises Grade 6 students in the Netherlands who participated in PIRLS-2016. The report indicates that 22 schools were included for the pilot and 150 schools for the main study, with additional reserve schools used to meet international response requirements; only countries meeting the minimum school participation and response thresholds are included in international comparisons. Students were tested in two 40-minute sessions and completed the student questionnaire; the report does not specify further analytic exclusions beyond noting that non-participation reasons (e.g., leaving school, parental objection, disability, insufficient Dutch) were recorded on the student follow-up form.

data.outcome_summary: This PIRLS-2016 Netherlands report describes Grade 6 reading proficiency and its associations with student, teacher, school, and home context factors. It uses PIRLS plausible values (five PVs derived via IRT) and reports weighted results for reading proficiency, with an overall Netherlands mean score of 545 (SE=1.7) and an international rank of 14th. The report finds that girls outperform boys, students who (nearly) always speak Dutch at home outperform those who sometimes/never do, and students with higher reading engagement, enjoyment, and self-confidence have higher reading scores. At the school level, reading proficiency is lowest in schools with higher shares of economically disadvantaged students and lower shares of Dutch first-language speakers, and rural schools score highest compared with urban schools. No machine-learning predictive modeling is performed; therefore, no ML algorithm performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are applicable, and the study should be interpreted as descriptive large-scale assessment analysis rather than causal inference.
